excerpt: A personal memory of the orderly fences outside Subic Naval Base opens a window into the final, serene days of Cañacao Naval Hospital in 1941. Through the eyes of U.S. Navy Nurse Dorothy Still Danner, The Fall of Canacao in 1941 captures the fragile calm of an island outpost—and the forty-five minutes of bombardment that shattered it forever.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
imageAlt: Dorothy Still and Eldene Paige comfort an internee who had fainted following their rescue rom the Los Banos camp. Photo taken by Carl Mydans
bodyText:
Visiting my cousin Beth in Olongapo City before college felt like stepping through a portal. Inside Subic Naval Base,the world shifted. The roads were spotless, drivers followed strict courtesy, and everything hummed with orderly discipline.

Without a dependent’s ID, I couldn't enter the commissary. So, I stayed back in a nearby shop. I treated people-watching like an Olympic sport and read an abandoned newspaper like I had struck gold. Standing in the shade, I watched base life unfold, catching glimpses of striking servicemen while my conservative upbringing kept my gaze strictly discreet.

![Dorothy Still Danner](/assets/uploads/cms/dorothy.jpg "Dorothy Still Danner portrait taken after WWII. US Navy/BUMED photo")

That tidy, restricted world stayed with me long after I left. Years later, when I read the oral history of Dorothy Still Danner—one of eleven U.S. Navy nurses captured in the Philippines—that afternoon outside the Subic commissary snapped into a much larger historical frame. Dorothy had lived inside that exact same world at Cañacao Naval Hospital across Manila Bay, long before the war tore it apart.

Cañacao was a 240-bed haven on a lobster-claw peninsula, nestled between the Navy Yard and the seaplanes at Sangley Point. Banyan trees shaded the grounds, and amber lights inside tiny lighthouses glowed along the seawall at dusk. Life followed a familiar rhythm: Monday meant recovering from liberty, Wednesday prepped for Thursday’s full-dress inspection, Friday readied the weekend, and Tuesday was for actual work. Dependents lived comfortably with local amahs, and evenings brought relaxed parties at the *comandancia*.

Then, the geopolitical barometer dropped. In early 1941, Admiral Thomas C. Hart ordered all military dependents sent home as regional tensions boiled. Hart was a relentless commander who drove his crews with endless drills.

Other crises hit closer to home. Late in 1941, a polio outbreak struck the sailors at Sangley Point. With the tuberculosis ward overflowing, the staff converted a schoolhouse into an emergency isolation ward, managing critical patients—including one trapped in an iron lung.

Even so, war felt distant. When news of Pearl Harbor reached the hospital at 3:00 a.m. on December 8, 1941, nurses moved through dark wards with blue-filtered flashlights, assuming it was just another drill.

The illusion shattered on December 10. At noon, Japanese high-altitude bombers struck Manila Bay, reducing the Navy Yard and hospital to rubble in forty-five minutes. Power failed, and casualties flooded the wards: sailors, civilians, and workers. Order vanished. With no time for clean linen or hesitation, Dorothy and her fellow nurses went straight to work. Cañacao had fallen. In the chaos, no orders arrived for their evacuation. The Navy nurses just kept going.

## **Evacuation to Manila**

Staying inside the ruined Cavite Navy Yard proved untenable within hours. Fires burned out of control, water mains were severed, and secondary explosions from ammunition dumps rattled the remaining walls. The medical staff made the urgent decision to evacuate their remaining patients across Manila Bay to Sternberg General Hospital, the U.S.Army's primary facility in the capital.

Transporting critically wounded men across shattered roads was a grueling endeavor. Ammunition trucks, civilian vehicles, and improvised ambulances hauled casualties through the smoke into Manila. Dorothy and her fellow nurses worked continuously during transit, monitoring blood loss and holding bandages over rough terrain. Recalling the chaotic influx, Dorothy noted:

> *"Triage was impossible. You just tried to find out which were the worst ones to go to surgery..."*

Upon arrival, Sternberg was already overwhelmed. Wards were packed to capacity, and stretchers lined the corridors.As Japanese forces advanced down the Luzon plain, Manila was declared an open city to spare it from total destruction.Military medical units were ordered to consolidate and convert civilian structures into emergency wards.

The nurses moved their patients once more, this time to the campus of Santa Scholastica’s College. Classrooms and concrete hallways became makeshift hospital wards almost overnight.

It was here that Chief Nurse Laura Cobb demonstrated sharp foresight. Recognizing that Japanese occupation forces would quickly seize medical stockpiles upon entry into Manila, Cobb ordered her nurses to relabel their essential pharmaceutical supplies. Standard bottles of quinine and other scarce anti-malarial medications were systematically transferred and re-marked with generic or harmless labels.

That quick thinking saved lives in the coming months. When Japanese troops eventually entered the compound to inventory supplies, the critical malaria drugs remained undetected in plain sight.

### Into Santo Tomas

On January 2, 1942, Japanese forces entered Manila. Technical status as non-combatant medical personnel offered no protection. On January 7, Japanese officers arrived at Santa Scholastica and officially interned the eleven Navy nurses,transporting them to the campus of Santo Tomas University.

The university grounds were transformed into a concentration camp for nearly four thousand civilian detainees. Canvas cots and wooden bunks sat side by side with bare inches between them.

For Dorothy and her colleagues, professional routines shifted immediately from military discipline to camp survival.Chief Nurse Laura Cobb organized the nurses into working shifts to staff the makeshift camp infirmary, treating dysentery, dengue fever, and malnutrition under severe resource constraints. The hidden reserves of quinine kept malaria cases from spiraling out of control across the camp population.

Daily existence settled into a static routine. Roll calls occurred twice daily, punctuated by strict bows to Japanese guards. Food rations began a steady decline in quantity and quality, turning meal times into exercises in precise rationing. Yet the nurses remained in uniform, preserving a sense of professional identity and purpose while waiting for a rescue that felt months away.

### Transfer to Los Baños

By mid-1943, Santo Tomas was bursting at the seams. To ease severe overcrowding, Japanese authorities resolved to construct a new internment camp forty miles south at an agricultural college in Los Baños, at the foot of Mount Makiling.

Chief Nurse Laura Cobb saw what was coming. Collaborating with Dr. Charles Leach, a fellow internee and Rockefeller Foundation physician, Cobb advocated strongly for the Navy nurses to be assigned to the new camp. She knew that carving a raw encampment out of the jungle lowlands would inevitably trigger widespread disease and physical collapse among the internee labor details.

In May 1944, the order came. The eleven Navy nurses were transferred south alongside hundreds of civilian internees.

The transit was brutal. Packed into stifling boxcars on the Manila Railroad, the prisoners traveled under heavy guard.Upon arrival, they found primitive wooden barracks, thatched roofs, and dirt floors in place of concrete university halls.

At Los Baños, hunger soon rivaled disease as the primary enemy. Rations were systematically slashed. Daily sustenance shrank to meager portions of unhusked rice, cassava, and weeds gathered along the perimeter wire.Malnutrition spread rapidly. Beriberi, scurvy, and severe weight loss affected nearly every internee.

Despite their own failing strength, Dorothy and her colleagues maintained daily clinical shifts. They treated tropical ulcers with limited antiseptics, boiled bandages for reuse, and monitored failing vital signs. Their presence provided a vital anchor for the camp.

### The Raid of February 23, 1945

![](/assets/uploads/cms/losbanosburning.jpg "")

By early 1945, liberation was a daily race against slow starvation inside the camp wire. On the night of February 22,Dorothy was working the night shift in the camp infirmary.

> *"I was on duty that night. There was a newborn baby and I was trying to feed her with what little powdered milk was left. The mother could hardly nurse the baby. She hadn't had enough nourishment herself..."*

At dawn on February 23, 1945, the sky above Los Baños filled with parachutes. In a synchronized attack, the 11th Airborne Division, combined with Filipino guerrillas, stormed the perimeter guards. As the firing subsided, amphibious tractors crashed through the camp fences.

> *"An amtrac pulled up in front of the hospital and American troops jumped out. We never saw anything so handsome in our lives. These fellows looked so healthy and so lively... This whole thing went off with just the most amazing precision that you could imagine."*

Within hours, all eleven Navy nurses and over 2,000 internees were evacuated across Laguna de Bay to safety. The eleven Sacred Eleven—who had held their duty through the fall of Cañacao, the crowded wards of Santa Scholastica,and the long darkness of internment—were finally going home.
